When you attempt something, you try to do it — but with a very important detail baked in: you are not sure you will succeed. There is a real possibility of failure, and you know it. You are making an effort toward a goal that is uncertain, difficult, or challenging.

That is the heart of the word. It is not just trying something casually. It carries a sense of deliberate effort against some difficulty or risk.
Breaking It Down with Simple Examples

She attempted to climb the mountain.

This tells you she put in real effort to climb it. But it does not tell you she reached the top. She may have succeeded, or she may have failed. The word "attempted" covers both possibilities — it only promises the effort, not the result.

Compare that to:

She climbed the mountain.

Now you know she succeeded. The action is complete and confirmed.

This contrast shows you something important: "attempt" focuses on the effort and the trying, not on whether the goal was achieved.

You would not normally say "I attempted to breathe" or "I attempted to blink." That would sound strange, because breathing and blinking are effortless — there is no real chance of failing at them.

"Attempt" naturally fits situations where:

  • The task is hard or demanding.
  • The outcome is uncertain.
  • There is a real chance of failing.
  • You are doing something brave, risky, or ambitious.

The scientist attempted to find a cure for the disease.
The student attempted every question on the exam, even the hardest ones.
He attempted to fix the broken engine, though he had no experience.
The negotiators attempted to reach a peace agreement.

In all of these, there is effort, there is difficulty, and the outcome is not guaranteed.

"Attempt" as a verb is used in two main ways:

1. Attempt + to + verb (infinitive)
This is the most common pattern.

She attempted to solve the puzzle.
They attempted to escape from the building.
He attempted to speak calmly, but his voice shook.

2. Attempt + a noun (a thing)
Here you attempt an action or task that is named as a noun.

She attempted the challenge.
He attempted the jump.
The team attempted a comeback in the final minutes.
She attempted an apology, but the words came out wrong.

Both patterns are correct. The first is more common in everyday use; the second is slightly more compact and often found in writing.
"Attempt" vs. "Try" — What Is the Real Difference?

These two words are close in meaning, and in many sentences, you can use either one. But there are subtle differences worth knowing.

"Try" is the everyday, neutral word. It is informal, versatile, and fits almost any situation — big or small, easy or hard.

Try the soup. Try turning it off and on again. Try to relax.

"Attempt" is more formal and more serious. It tends to be used when:

  • The task is more significant, difficult, or ambitious.
  • The context is professional, academic, legal, or official.
  • You want to emphasize deliberate, conscious effort.
  • The possibility of failure feels more real or more weighty.

The surgeon attempted a complex procedure that had never been done before.
(More natural than: The surgeon tried a complex procedure... — though "tried" still works.)

Please attempt all questions in Section B.
(Formal instruction, as on an exam paper.)

He attempted to deceive the court.
(Legal or serious context — sounds more precise and grave than "He tried to deceive the court," though both are grammatically correct.)

In short: "try" is your casual everyday word; "attempt" is its more formal, more serious cousin. When in doubt in informal conversation, "try" is fine. When writing formally or describing something genuinely difficult and significant, "attempt" fits better.

This is very important. The word "attempt" says nothing about success. It is completely neutral about the result. You must always read the rest of the sentence or context to find out what happened.

She attempted to open the lock. — Did she open it? We don't know yet.
She attempted to open the lock, but failed. — She did not open it.
She attempted to open the lock, and succeeded. — She opened it.

Without extra information, "attempted" only confirms: she made an effort. Nothing more, nothing less.

This is actually why "attempt" is such a precise word. It separates the act of trying from the result of trying — two things that are, in reality, always separate.

Because "attempt" is tied to difficulty and uncertainty, it often carries a slight feeling of courage, determination, or seriousness. When you say someone "attempted" something, you are subtly acknowledging that it was not easy, that it took effort, and that failure was a real possibility they faced.

Against all odds, she attempted to save the failing business.

This sentence carries respect for her effort, regardless of whether she ultimately saved the business.

It can also be used in a neutral or even critical tone, depending on context:

He attempted an explanation, but it only confused everyone further.

Here, "attempted" quietly signals that the explanation did not work well — it was tried, but it fell short.

• Attempt a task / attempt a question — to try to complete it, especially in a formal or academic setting.
  • Attempt a record — to try to break a record (sports, achievements).
  • Attempt an escape — to try to escape (often used in dramatic, serious, or legal contexts).
  • Attempt a smile / attempt a joke — to try to do something social or emotional, often when it doesn't come easily.
  • Attempt the impossible — to try to do something that seems cannot be done.
A Quick Summary to Tie It All Together

To attempt means to make a deliberate, conscious effort to do something — especially something difficult, risky, or uncertain — without any guarantee of success.

It is more formal than "try." It emphasizes real effort. It says nothing about whether you succeeded. And it fits best when the task has genuine difficulty or weight behind it.

The next time you see or hear "attempted," ask yourself: Who was trying? What were they trying to do? Was it hard? Did they succeed? The word "attempted" answers the first three questions on its own — the last one, you will need the context to find.
